analytical_models.equation_role: Compute KIC from indentation modulus, hardness, load and average crack length: KIC = 0.016 (E/HV)^(1/2) · P / c^(2/3)
analytical_models.model_note: The listed E, HV and c values are those of the 15Al peak-hardness sample (965.6 HV, aged at 600 °C for 6 h), not this 600 °C/10 h sample, since KIC was evaluated on the hardest samples.

parameters.name: c (average crack length, c = 0.25 Σ l_i)

computational_details.validation_against_experiment: KIC calculated from measured indentation crack lengths; KIC values of the hardest samples of the 15Al, 17Al and 19Al alloys were 8.6, 6.6 and 3.5 MPa·m^1/2 respectively.

defect_interactions.interaction_type: FCC twins within the Cu-rich particles
defect_interactions.qualitative_or_quantitative_description: The fine FCC Cu-rich particles at the β-Mn interfaces exhibited an FCC crystalline structure with FCC twins frequently observed within the particles (TEM of the 15Al peak-hardness sample, 600 °C / 6 h).

interfaces.interface_notes: The new BCC phase at the β-Mn interfaces forms from enrichment of the BCC-stabilizing element Al around the β-Mn interfaces; the FCC Cu-rich phase forms due to the limited solubility of Cu in Fe-based alloys and expulsion of Cu from the β-Mn during precipitation and growth. TEM/EDS evidence (β-Mn + FCC Cu-rich interfaces) was obtained on the 15Al alloy aged at 600 °C for 6 h (peak-hardness sample).
interfaces.phase_evolution: α → α + FCC Cu-rich phase → α-Mn + β-Mn + BCC phase → β-Mn + BCC phase + FCC Cu-rich phase

processing_steps.processing_steps_notes: Alloy ingots with nominal composition Fe-35Mn-15Al-5Cu (at.%) produced by melting high-purity (>99.9 %) raw materials in a vacuum induction furnace under an argon atmosphere. Chemical composition of the 15Al alloy (Table 1, EDS): Fe 44.6, Mn 35.2, Al 15.0, Cu 5.2 (at.%).
Ingots homogenized at 1200 °C for 24 h prior to hot rolling.
Hot-rolled into plates with a thickness of 4 mm; then cut into 10 × 5 × 2 mm^3 samples by electrical discharge machining.

Solution treated at 1100 °C for 10 min under an argon atmosphere, followed by oil quenching. This is the parent process (proc_st-1100c-10min-oq); the solution-treated baseline Vickers hardness of the 15Al alloy is 253.4 ± 2.1 HV.
The solution-treated 15Al sample was aged at 600 °C for 10 h, followed by water quenching (target condition for this sample).

measurement_conditions.other_conditions: 15Al alloy aged at 600 °C for 10 h; Vickers hardness measured with a load of 9.8 N for 15 s, average of 5 measurements
Measured through compressive stress-strain curves for the 15Al alloy

structures.overall_structure: Solution-treated 15Al Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steel consists of a single α (body-centred cubic, BCC) phase; no γ (FCC) phase is resolved in the EBSD phase maps. The 15Al solution-treated grains are coarse (a few very large grains).

After aging at 600 °C (for this sample 10 h) the α matrix of the 15Al alloy had almost completely transformed to β-Mn (the α → β-Mn transformation completes within ~1 h at 600 °C and above), forming a near-equiaxed β-Mn matrix. Abundant fine precipitates are distributed at/within the β-Mn: an FCC Cu-rich phase and a new BCC phase.

unmapped_findings: For the 15Al alloy, the maximum Vickers hardness of 965.6 ± 7.6 HV was achieved after aging at 600 °C for 6 h (a shorter time than this sample's 10 h); after reaching the peak, extending the aging time to 10 h slightly decreased the hardness to 948.6 ± 12.8 HV (this sample's value). The 600 °C series is the highest among all aging temperatures for the 15Al alloy (Fig. 2).

The α → β-Mn transformation of the 15Al alloy is complete (α matrix almost fully transformed) within about 1 h of aging at 600 °C and above, and in only ~3 h at 525 °C; the resulting ultra-hard β-Mn gives the alloy its ultra-high hardness (253.4 HV solution-treated → up to 965.6 HV).

TEM/SAED/EDS analyses were performed only on the 15Al alloy aged at 600 °C for 6 h (the peak-hardness sample, not this 600 °C/10 h sample): it showed near-equiaxed β-Mn, fine FCC Cu-rich particles (rich in Cu, depleted in Fe and Mn, slightly poor in Al) with FCC twins at the β-Mn interfaces, and Cu-poor β-Mn.

Nanoindentation results pertain to the 15Al peak-hardness sample (600 °C/6 h): average nanohardness 11.7 ± 0.4 GPa and intrinsic β-Mn hardness 12.1 ± 0.3 GPa; SEM-EDS of β-Mn in that sample gave Al 14.3, Mn 36.8, Cu 2.8 at.%.

Fracture toughness data pertain to the hardest 15Al sample (peak hardness 965.6 HV, reached at 600 °C/6 h, not this 10 h sample): average indentation crack length 18 μm and KIC = 8.6 MPa·m^1/2 (E = 164 GPa). The KIC of the ultra-hard Fe-Mn-Al-Cu low-density steels decreases with increasing Al content (8.6, 6.6, 3.5 MPa·m^1/2 for 15Al, 17Al, 19Al).

The specific hardness of the Fe-35.2Mn-15Al-5.2Cu (15Al) alloy reaches 141 HV·cm^3/g at its peak-hardness condition; existing steels and medium/high entropy alloys generally have specific hardness below 120 HV·cm^3/g.
